lessons.question: Your slide says the system saves five hours. Which missing detail could completely change what that claim means?
options: The font used on the slide
The review effort and case volume behind it
lessons.explanation: Hours saved mean little if review work grew or the volume was tiny. A claim is only usable when the reviewer can see what it was measured against.

lessons.after: Organise the submission so a reviewer
lessons.question: A reviewer cannot tell which files you wrote and which the system produced. Which evidence-pack rule was missed?
options: Start with the problem and intended users
Keep source files and generated outputs distinguishable
lessons.explanation: If inputs and outputs are mixed, a reviewer cannot check a claim against its evidence. Clear separation lets them move from claim to proof.

lessons.after: The course's practical rubric weights weekly work
lessons.question: A learner earns 80% of the capstone component. How many percentage points does that add to their overall practical result?
lessons.explanation: The capstone is weighted at 45%, so 0.8 × 45 = 36 points. It is the largest single component of the practical rubric.

lessons.after: "Adopt for internal draft preparation for one team
lessons.prompt: Which kind of decision does each statement describe?

items.text: One team, mandatory review, monthly cost cap
Names the blocking issue and its owner
Explains why further implementation is not justified
Reassess after fifty more cases or a model change

lessons.explanation: Each decision type has its own content. An adopt sets limits and review triggers, a revise says what must change, and a stop explains why to end.

lessons.prompt: In a five-minute demo, how much time would you give to things going wrong? Make a guess before revealing.
lessons.answer: About two minutes: one on a failure and its handling, one on a blocked action and recovery. Showing limits is part of the evidence, not a distraction from it.

lessons.prompt: Put the five one-minute demo segments in the recommended order.
lessons.explanation: The audience needs the baseline to judge normal operation, and needs to see limits before they can trust the recommendation that closes the demo.

lessons.after: Choose a failure relevant to the project.
lessons.question: During your demo, someone changes the payload of an action that was already approved. What should happen?
options: It sends, because approval was given
lessons.explanation: Approval belongs to an exact payload. A changed payload is effectively a new action, so it must go back for approval.

lessons.after: Be ready to explain why you selected
lessons.prompt: Why might a reviewer ask you to explain one thing the AI suggested that you changed?
lessons.answer: It shows you understand your system's behaviour and limits, rather than accepting generated work unexamined. You do not need every library API memorised, but you must own the design decisions.

lessons.prompt: The course is over and you want to keep improving. What makes a good next experiment? Think, then reveal.
lessons.answer: Investigate one measured limitation. Pick a single experiment, compare it with the strongest simple baseline, and keep the same discipline of evidence, boundaries and operational ownership.

lessons.after: Reproduce the final candidate from its documented setup
lessons.prompt: Which route does each final task belong to?

items.text: Reproduce the candidate from its version record
Show how staff reject an action and stop the workflow
Hand over the repository and maintenance ownership
Explain the next improvement and its evidence

lessons.explanation: Engineers prove the system can be rebuilt and maintained; business owners prove staff and budget holders can run and govern it.

lessons.after: Verify the workflow, staff procedure, review
lessons.question: Which three roles does the business-owner route ask you to name for future changes?
options: Operational owner, budget owner and reviewer
Model provider, platform vendor and user
lessons.explanation: Someone must run it, someone must pay for it, and someone must check changes. Naming them keeps the system governed after the builder steps away.

lessons.after: Submit every item in [the capstone checklist]
lessons.question: You are a self-directed learner and no independent peer reviews your evidence. How should you label your practical assessment?
lessons.explanation: Without an independent peer, the honest label is self-reviewed. Claiming more would overstate what the evidence shows.
